title: How Much Faster Does AI Actually Make Programmers?

sentences.text: How much faster does AI actually make the people who write code?

onScreenText: How much faster does AI make the people who write code?

sentences.text: Ask around and the answers point in opposite directions, from enormous multiples to slower than before.
So set the loudest answers aside, look at the studies that measured programmers at work, and ask what each one actually measured.

onScreenText: From enormous multiples to slower than before

sentences.text: On the Lex Fridman Podcast, DHH described "that magical 10X, 100X, in a few rare cases, 1000X productivity boost", and said that to get it you have to work with the AI agents directly.

sentences.text: From the other side, a run of videos and posts repeats one trial's result, in the words of the channel Macro Lens: when experienced developers were allowed AI tools, "they were 19% slower than when they weren't".

sentences.text: Start with ordinary workplaces.

One set of field experiments followed almost five thousand software developers at three companies, in their regular jobs and partly over years, and estimated that an AI code suggestion tool raised their productivity, measured by their output, by about 26 percent.

The authors note that this is substantially smaller than an earlier lab result, and suggest why: some kinds of coding are less readily helped by the tool, and coding is only part of a developer's job.

sentences.text: A separate trial estimated a roughly 21 percent increase in development speed attributable to AI, but that estimate missed the usual bar for statistical significance, so it is less certain than it sounds.

sentences.text: Then there is the trial behind those slowdown claims.

onScreenText: The trial behind the slowdown claims

sentences.text: METR ran a randomized controlled trial with 16 experienced open-source developers on 246 tasks in mature projects they had worked on for an average of 5 years, randomly allowing or disallowing AI tools task by task.
The tools were the February to June 2025 frontier: mostly the Cursor Pro editor with Claude 3.5 and 3.7 Sonnet.

chart.title: METR randomized controlled trial, February to June 2025

points.label: Years of prior experience on the project, average

chart.note: AI allowed or disallowed at random, task by task.

sentences.text: With AI allowed, tasks took 19 percent longer to complete.

chart.title: With AI allowed
chart.note: Early-2025 tools, experienced developers on their own mature projects.

sentences.text: The researchers' hypothesis for why AI helped less than in earlier trials: their projects averaged about 10 years old and more than 1,100,000 lines of code, compared with the more greenfield projects in those trials.

chart.title: The projects in the METR trial, average
chart.note: A hypothesis from the researchers, not a measured cause.

sentences.text: But would newer tools change that?
METR's own 2026 update says that, from talking to participants, it believes developers are likely more sped up in early 2026 than in early 2025.

excerpt.text:
Based on conversations with study participants, we believe it is likely that developers are more sped up from AI tools now — in early 2026 — compared to our estimates from early 2025. However, because of the selection effects in our experiment, our data is only very weak evidence for the size of this increase.
Our raw results show some evidence for speedup. Our early 2025 study found the use of AI causes tasks to take 19% longer, with a confidence interval between +2% and +39%. For the subset of the original developers who participated in the later study, we now estimate a speedup of -18% with a confidence interval between -38% and +9%. Among newly-recruited developers the estimated speedup is -4%, with a confidence interval between -15% and +9%.
excerpt.highlight: we believe it is likely that developers are more sped up from AI tools now

sentences.text: Its new raw numbers lean the same way: tasks took an estimated 18 percent less time for returning developers and 4 percent less for new recruits, but both ranges still stretch to a slowdown.

chart.title: METR 2026, estimated cut in task time with AI
chart.note: Both confidence intervals reach +9%, a slowdown.

sentences.text: And METR calls this only very weak evidence: more developers now decline to take part because they don't want to work without AI, which likely pushes its speedup estimate down, so the ones left are not a fair sample.

excerpt.text:
METR previously published a paper which found the use of AI tools caused a 20% slowdown in completing tasks among experienced open-source developers, using data from February to June 2025.
To understand how AI is impacting developer productivity over time, we started a new experiment in August 2025 with a larger pool of developers using the latest AI tools.
Unfortunately, given participant feedback and surveys, we believe that the data from our new experiment gives us an unreliable signal of the current productivity effect of AI tools. The primary reason is that we have observed a significant increase in developers choosing not to participate in the study because they do not wish to work without AI, which likely biases downwards our estimate of AI-assisted speedup. We additionally believe there have been selection effects due to a lower pay rate (we reduced the pay from $150/hr to $50/hr), and that our measurements of time-spent on each task are unreliable for the fraction of developers who use multiple AI agents concurrently.
Based on conversations with study participants, we believe it is likely that developers are more sped up from AI tools now — in early 2026 — compared to our estimates from early 2025. However, because of the selection effects in our experiment, our data is only very weak evidence for the size of this increase.
Our raw results show some evidence for speedup. Our early 2025 study found the use of AI causes tasks to take 19% longer, with a confidence interval between +2% and +39%. For the subset of the original developers who participated in the later study, we now estimate a speedup of -18% with a confidence interval between -38% and +9%. Among newly-recruited developers the estimated speedup is -4%, with a confidence interval between -15% and +9%.
excerpt.highlight: developers choosing not to participate in the study because they do not wish to work without AI

sentences.text: And the multiples from the start?

onScreenText: And the multiples from the start?

sentences.text: The largest figures so far come from Anthropic's own report on its staff: employees self-reported that they now get a 50 percent productivity gain from Claude on average, and merged pull requests per engineer per day rose 67 percent when its engineering org adopted Claude Code.
A count of merged changes is not the same as time saved, but even taken at face value, both figures are an order of magnitude below ten times.

points.label: Merged pull requests per engineer per day

chart.note: Self-report and a count of merged changes, not measured time saved.

citations.label: Anthropic, How AI is transforming work at Anthropic

sentences.text: So, how much faster? In the workplace studies, with the tools they tested, the measured gains were modest, nowhere near the multiples in the hype.
For experienced developers in big, mature projects they knew well, early-2025 tools made them slower, and whether today's tools have reversed that, METR's own newer data is too weak to say.

citations.label: Cui, Demirer et al.; Google trial

sentences.text: But that slowdown trial holds a stranger detail, and it is about what the developers believed was happening.
Take a second and make your own guess: how much time does AI save you?

onScreenText: How much time does AI save you?

sentences.text: Before starting, the METR developers forecast that allowing AI would cut their completion time by 24 percent.
After the study, with the work behind them, they estimated it had cut their time by 20 percent, in the same trial that measured them taking longer.
Outside experts did no better: economists predicted 39 percent shorter completion times, and machine learning experts 38 percent.

chart.title: Predicted cut in completion time, METR trial
chart.note: Measured: tasks took 19% longer with AI.

sentences.text: So people overestimate the gain? Not always.

In an earlier randomized trial of Copilot, a lab task on a greenfield-style project, the measured productivity gain was 55.8 percent, yet participants in both the AI and the control group estimated 35 percent on average: they underestimated it.

chart.title: Copilot lab trial: productivity gain
chart.note: One lab task on a greenfield-style project.

citations.label: Peng et al., Copilot randomized trial

sentences.text: So the same kind of guess missed in opposite directions: too high for experienced developers in big projects they knew well, too low on a fresh task in the lab.

citations.label: Peng et al., Copilot randomized trial

sentences.text: METR's later update adds that some developers now self-report very high speedups, and repeats that, as its earlier study found, such estimates can be quite unreliable.

excerpt.text: However the true speedup could be much higher among the developers and tasks which are selected out of the experiment. Some developers self-report very high speedups, though as we documented in our earlier study those estimates can be quite unreliable.
excerpt.highlight: those estimates can be quite unreliable

sentences.text: So can developers tell? In both of these trials, not reliably: their guesses missed by a wide margin.

citations.label: Peng et al., Copilot randomized trial

sentences.text: Every number in this video belongs to particular people, doing particular work, with particular tools.

So when someone tells you how much faster AI makes them, ask what they measured, and if you want to know for yourself, time comparable tasks with the tool and without it rather than trusting the feeling.
